title: How hard to lean on the old seed

data.source: Stein (1956), James and Stein (1961), Robbins (1956), Efron and Morris (1973); cited from memory. Simulated Gaussian contents, seeded.

prediction: The seed rule is a linear shrinkage rule. Stein's theory sets the pull q from the data at 1/(1 + T), where T is the scatter of true contents over the noise; a fixed q = 0.618 is best only at T = 0.618, beats using no seed only below T = 2.236, and is 9.69 times worse at T = 25.
baseline: Stein (1956), James and Stein (1961), Efron and Morris (1973): the James-Stein estimator and the oracle pull 1/(1 + T). Decoy: q = 0.5.
relation: a special case: shrinkage with the amount left free
status_line: CRR here is: a special case of shrinkage estimation with the amount left free; Stein's theory sets q from the data, and 0.618 is the best pull only when the scatter of true contents is 0.618 of the noise.
why: R5's flat seed rule (Phoenix status ASSUMPTION) pulls each new mark toward the old seed by the fraction q, which is linear shrinkage. James-Stein reads the pull off the data and was better than no seed at every scatter tried. A fixed 0.618 was better than no seed only for scatter below 2.236 and matched the best possible pull only at 0.618. R5's own words, 'there is no universal value of q', are what the theorems say; the working value 0.618 is a choice, not an optimum.
